STATE ROAD SECTOR  
State Road Network – Review of Progress and Constraints Faced  
67. The Ministry has submitted that State Highways (SHs) and Major District Roads (MDRs) 
constitute the secondary system of road transportat ion in the country. Their total length SHs 
stands at about 1,54,000 km and that of MDRs is est imated at around 300,000 km. State roads 
carry heavy to medium traffic. It is assessed that the secondary system carries about 40 percent of 
the total road traffic.  Their present condition an d stage of development varies widely from state 
to state. The status of MDRs is particularly worris ome. One of the main reason for this is that the 
funds made available for these roads are inadequate . Against requirement of Rs.25,000 crores per 
annum, a total amount of only Rs. 8,000 crores per annum is being made available.  Some of the 
major constraints faced by different States in the execution of the programmes for state roads 
during the 11thPlan are – (i) Lack of Policy and Pl anning, (ii) Control on Pre-construction 
Activities, (iii) Capacity Constraints, (iv) Lack o f Finances, and (v) Need for further 
strengthening Consultancy and Contracting Industry.  There is lack of data base in the road sector. 
This needs to be strengthened with support from MoRTH and IRC.  
PLANNING FOR STATE HIGHWAY DEVELOPMENT PROJECT  
68. There is a need now to identify a CORE NETWORK of major arterial routes. It is 
important that Core road network should have a Corr idor Concept. Holistic planning in this 
corridor needs to be done where necessary, involvin g SH and MDR under this concept. It should 
be possible for traffic to move at an average speed  of 60-70 km per hour, so that commercial 
vehicles being the carriers of economy can cover a distance of 500 to 600 km in one day.  The 
“Core Network” of State Roads should, essentially, comprise of  SHs and MDRs, which have 
high volumes of traffic or have such potential.   
69. The Committee observes that the picture of State Hi ghways projected by the 
Ministry is not very encouraging.  The Committee fe els that State Highways are bridge 
16

 
between National Highways and people.  Development of any State depends on good roads.  
The Ministry can also provide its expertise in road  development  and planning.  The 
Committee recommends that NHAI and State Govt. shou ld work in co-ordination while 
planning for highways as it forms the life of the c ore network.  The Committee agrees with 
the Ministry’s approach that priority may be given for development of core network.   The 
Committee feels that there is a requirement of Nati onal Mission for development of State 
roads.  The funding to the State Govt. by the Centr al Govt. may be linked to the 
maintenance and construction good State Roads.  The  Committee recommends that the 
Central Govt. should take initiative to create a da ta bank of State roads and District to 
enable the planning and execution of projects. 
URBAN LINKAGES TO NATIONAL EXPRESSWAYS NETWORK  
70. The Committee was informed that it is important  to provide urban linkages to National 
Expressways  Network or to any inter-city Expresswa ys developed by the State Governments. 
These should also desirably be access controlled fa cilities  wherever required and feasible. For 
this purpose, the Road Authorities responsible for Urban Road Development shall have to be 
associated. An integrated scheme may be evolved and  implemented parallel to address the 
specific requirements to provide Urban Connectivity  under a separate initiative involving 
Planning Commission, concerned State Governments and the concerned Road Authorities besides 
M/o Urban Development and M/o Road Transport & High ways with clear identification of the 
roles and responsibilities of each organization to obviate implementation difficulties, etc. The 
State Governments shall have to be primarily respon sible for development of these Urban 
Linkages. Feasibility shall have to be explored to develop these Urban Linkages on PPP mode. 
For the sake of estimation, it is presumed that 50 % of total length would be implemented through 
budgetary allocation. The balance 50 % length would  be implemented through private sector 
participation on PPP mode. For the projects to be t aken up on PPP mode, about 30 % of project 
cost is assumed to be met from budgetary allocation s towards payment of VGF, etc. and balance 
70 % is to be mobilized by private sector. 
71. The Committee observes that urban linkages is a n essential part of road network, 
without which the purpose of highways will be defea ted.  The Committee agrees with the 
Ministry envisaging the need of integrated scheme in co-ordination with Ministries of Urban 
Development, Road Transport and Highways and State Govt. for urban linkages. 
72. But the Committee in view of past experience in  this sector would caution the 
Ministry while exploring the chance of developing u rban linkages on PPP mode as this 
mode has not been quite a success.  The Committee e xpects the Ministry to come up with 
concrete solution to meet the existing challenges without any financial problem. 
73. The total network of SHs and MDRs should be ide ntified by each State as a long term 
vision (say by 2031). The policy should be to cover the entire “Core Network” under this 
programme as far as possible.  In relation to protection of environment the Concept of Green 
Highways is another initiative that can be appropriately planned and designed. States may take up 
some Pilot projects and implement the same.

75. The Central Government has created a window for  providing viability gap funding (VGF) 
upto an amount of 20 percent of the project cost. A dditional cost of 20% of project cost can be 
provided by the State Government to the private entrepreneur. By a careful concession design and 
phased approach for development, it should be possi ble to cover some part of SHDP through 
private sector financing by leveraging the budgetar y resources. SHDP would need the support of 
the government budget. For this, the support of the  World Bank/ADB towards financing of these 
roads needs to continue. Preparing a blue print of identified major state road sections for PPP/PSP 
will help the states to achieve its’ part financing  needs. Implementing the projects would enable 
states to achieve its growth objectives.  Some stat es could consider taking up high traffic density 
road and bridge projects through tolls (rates of to ll should be affordable by road users. and award 
them to private entrepreneurs for a fixed concession period of say 15 years. This would relieve the 
state from maintenance of such projects as the obli gation will get passed on to the private 
entrepreneur. However, this would vary state to state and depending on willingness to pay.   
76. The Committee feels that implementation of Stat e Roads through private Sector 
financing is a right step in positive direction.  I t will attract developers since 40% fund of 
total project cost is to be contributed by the cent ral as well as by State Govt.

77. The Committee is of the view that the latest te chnology in this sector is with the 
Ministry and it can guide and help developers throu gh NHAI to carry out the projects.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should play active role in helping States at every 
stage of the project.

lack of funds made available for maintenance as per norms. They do not exceed 60% of normal 
requirements for main roads . Maintenance being a non-plan activity there is also a tendency

addressed to prevent premature failure of sections of NHs developed at large capital investments 
on account of self-accumulation of deficiencies due  to thin spreading of available resources for

further upgradation in say within about 4 ~ 9 year period.

maintenance system to be adopted for non NHDP developed reaches as well which

112. The Ministry has informed at present National Highways with aggregate length of 8480

maintained by the Ministry on Agency basis. A speci fic programme has also been initiated by the 
Central Government for the accelerated development of roads in the region covering about  
10,140 km length of National Highways, State roads and GS roads under ‘Special Accelerated 
Road Development Programme in North-East’ (SARDP-NE ) including Arunachal Package.  Also 
development of the balance works under East-West corridor and NHDP-Phase-III shall have to be 
completed in the 12th Plan.  Leaving apart the abov e, development of balance length of about  
1,766 km length of NHs may be taken up under NH(O) scheme of MORT&H as per availability 
of funds and inter-se priority.  
Special Needs and Strategies for the North East Region   
113. Roads are the principal modes of transport in the NE Region. The share of road transport 
would be well over 90 percent in the total movement  by surface transport in the Region. The 
riding quality and condition of main roads is generally fair to poor. The position is much  worse in 
case of State Highways and Major District Roads. On ly about 10 percent of the state highways 
can be said to be structurally adequate to carry th e legally permissible single axle load. Due to 
financial constraints, the states have not been abl e to provide strengthening overlays in any 
significant manner. From safety consideration, seve ral sections of single-lane roads need to be 
widened to two lanes of carriageway. The states may  need support to undertake a special  
programme of IRQP (Improvement in Riding Quality Pr ogramme) on the lines of National 
Highways. It needs to be  recognised that construct ion cost per kilometre is maximum whereas 
possibility of private financing is minimal and res ources available with the NE states is low. 
Hence infusion of central fund is a must.   Another  problem unique to the NE region is the 
presence of a number of semi-permanent timber bridg es. An accelerated program of replacing 
these bridges is to be implemented. Safety also needs to be 
enhanced by taking several engineering measures.  T he State Public Works Departments (PWDs) 
are responsible for policy, planning, design, const ruction and maintenance of state roads. They 
lack exposure to good practices in other states of the country and outside and need training.  
There are no state level or regional level training  centres except for Assam where the state level 
road research laboratory is being refurbished and s trengthened for training of PWD personnel. 
The Region depends basically upon the IAHE. There i s also a need to develop core faculty from 
within the Region also for which a scheme of traini ng the trainers should be prepared and 
implemented.

where improvement of about 10,141km road of various  category were identified for improvement

AMENITIES  
116. It is important that the wayside amenities be integrally planned and developed along with 
Expressways and all projects for 4-laning / 6-laning of NHs. Due provision is required to be made 
for LA, etc. while conceptualizing and preparing su ch projects. If the project is to be developed 
on BOT (Toll) basis, the concessionaire may develop  the facilities and operate the same during 
the concession period or even after that. For proje cts developed through BOT(Annuity), 
Concessionaire may develop the facilities and the G overnment may consider entrusting operation 
and maintenance of the facilities through private p articipation.  For projects developed through 
GBS funding, the facilities may be integrally devel oped by the Government and entrusted to 
private sector for operation and maintenance. Broad ly, the Integrated Way-side amenities may 
have following features: - 
(i) Facilities to be owned by Government operating / construction agencies. 
(ii) Operation & maintenance of individual facilities in  the wayside amenities through lease 
on profit sharing basis with private companies. 
(iii)Earmark certain facilities in the wayside amen ities exclusively to encourage local small 
scale producer on subsidy basis. 
(iv) Due consideration for preservation of ecology and e nvironment including recycling of 
waste water and harnessing of alternative sources o f energy (e.g. solar energy) for 
captive use.

 The Committee recommends that NHAI particularly mu st make all out efforts to 
complete these delayed projects.

completed within stipulated time without any hindrance.

REPORT 
The Ministry of Shipping encompasses within its fold the port and shipping 
sectors which include major ports, shipbuilding and ship -repair, national water -ways 
and inland water transport. The Ministry  has been entrusted with the responsibility to 
formulate policies and programmes on these subjects and their implementation. 
2. The following subordinate/attached offices, autonomous organizations, 
societies/associations and public sector undertakings are functioning under the 
administrative control of the Ministry of Shipping. 
 Directorate   General   of   Shipping,   Mumbai   (including   Minor   Ports   
Survey  Organization, Mumbai) 
 Andaman & Lakshadweep Harbour Works, Port Blair.  
 Directorate General of Lighthouses & Lightships, NOIDA  
 Port Trusts at Kolkata, Kochi (Cochin Port Trust), Kandla, Chennai, Mormugao, 
Mumbai, Nhava Sheva (Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust), Paradip, Tuticorin(V.O. 
Chidambaranar Port Trust), Visakhapatnam and New Mangalore.  
 Dock Labour Board at Kolkata  
 Inland Waterways Authority of India, Noida.  
 Tariff Authority for Major Ports, Mumbai.  
 Seamen‟s Provident Fund Organization, Mumbai.  
 Indian Maritime University.

the Ministry. The Committee examined the budget documents of the Ministry and the

7. The Committee notes from this table two trends – (i) there has been only 
marginal increments in the GBS to the Ministry every year and (ii) this GBS has 
been invariably reduced at RE stage every year.  Taking a realistic view, if 
expenditure is taken in terms of RE allocation, its percentage has been satisfactory 
and as per the financial norms.  It means that Ministry has shown  its capability to 
spend the finds given to it every ye ar.  The Committee, however, fails to 
understand,  how the Ministry of Finance could with such a good expenditure, 
allocate funds to Ministry of Shipping with a marginal increase every year.  In 
other words,  may be, if it  is given more  funds which shipp ing sector needs badly, 
the Ministry could have fruitfully used it.  The Committee in view of the potential 
and capabilities of Shipping sector in our economy in days to come, recommends 
that Ministry of Finance must increase GBS to Ministry of Shipping every year 
substantially. 
2

8. The Committee further observes that the non -plan expenditure is also has 
been good showing above 95% spending during the last 4 years except during 
2013-14 which was 85.86% of the RE.   
9. The Committee further observes that the IEBR gross expenditure stands 
only at 59.35% which also steadily decreased in the first three years.  As in the 
case of Plan allocation IEBR has also shown improvement during 2015 -16.  But, 
still more needs to be done. 
10. In the case of IEBR Committee not es that it has registered consistent 
decline from 2013 -14 on words.  Similarly, IEBR were reduced each year, except 
in 2012 -13, at RE stage; reduction being about 35 to 40%.  Needless to add, 
expenditure of IEBR also had declined and its percentage was not  as good as in 
the case of GBS.  Such a negative variation in case of IEBR shows that the 
performance of our ports and shipping sector need to be examined to find out real 
reasons for decline in generation of internal resources/revenue.  While good 
expenditure of GBS may indicates good performance, declining IEBR generation 
tells opposite story.  The Committee would like to know reasons for this and 
recommends the Ministry of Shipping make all out efforts for correcting this 
situation as shipping sector is going to face tremendous challenge in coming days.

18. The Committee observes that compared to 2015 -16, the allocation in 2016 -
17 for the Major Ports have been highly insufficient.  As per the projection made 
by the Ministry, they demanded Rs.467.48 crore whereas the allocation is a very 
meager amount of Rs.29.01 crore, which wil l adversely affect the 
modernization/capacity enhancement projects of the Tuticorin, Chennai and 
Mormugao Ports.  The Committee recommends that additional allocation for the 
ports may be made at RE Stage. 
19. The Committee further observes that the IWT Sec tor is a very important 
and emerging Sector which will be able to generate sufficient cargo and passenger 
movement in a very economical manner compared to other modes of transport.  In 
such a scenario, allocating only Rs.350.00 crore where demand stands at  
Rs.2384.00 crore is not helping the IWT Sector in a big way.  The Committee also 
understands that the Jal Marg Vikas project will be affected due to insufficient 
allocation.  The Committee recommends for more allocation for the IWT Sector. 
20. The Committee understands that the Ministry of Shipping has completed 
preparatory project development work related to port modernization; coastal 
shipping, coastal berths, IWT and ALHW, which needs additional funds for 
completion of the projects.  The Committee recom mends that the Ministry of 
Finance may look into the matter in view of the importance of the infrastructure 
development in the Port and Shipping Sectors; and sufficient funds may be 
allocated for these projects this year. 
21. The Committee also recommends for granting additional funds for the 
IMU in order to meet the committed liabilities of the approved projects.

25. The Ministry of Shipping during the deliberation informed that allocation of 
only Rs. 29 crore has been made in BE 2016 -17 under Plan for Major Ports. This 
allocation is inadequate t o meet the committed liabilities and additional requirement of 
Rs.388.61crore is needed in 2016-17 detailed as under: 
I. Mormugao Port Trust – Port connectivity project:  The Work of Port 
Connectivity is executed by the State Government of Goa. MormugaoPort ha s 
to provide its share of Rs.171 crore out of which Rs. 75 crore has already been 
released to the port in 2014 -15. In BE 2016 -17 an amount of Rs. 30 crore was 
proposed against which allocation of only Rs. 5 crore has been allocated. 
Additional requirement of Rs.25 crore is needed in 2016-17. 
II. Chennai Port Trust – Coastal road protection work:  Out of total cost of the 
project of Rs.63 crore, Rs.25 crore was released to the Chennai Port Trust upto 
2015-16. Till March, 2016 more than Rs. 35 crore has been spent  and the work 
is likely to be completed by December, 2016. Allocation of Rs. 5 crore in BE 
2016-17 is inadequate to make payment even with respect to the expenditure 
incurred upto 31.03.2016. As work is going on in full swing, non -availability of 
remaining funds would affect the completion of work in time. Additional 
requirement of Rs. 33crore is needed in 2016-17. 
III. V.O. Chidambaranar Port Trust (VOCPT) –Project relating to capital dredging 
in front of North Cargo Berth (NCB) II:  50% of the cost of the project which is 
about Rs. 224 crore is to be borne by the Government of India. Out of 
Government‟s committed liability, Rs. 89 crore has already been reimbursed to 
the port and the balance amount of Rs.135 crore is yet to be reimbursed. 
Additional requirement of Rs.120 crore is needed in 2016-17. 
IV. Cochin Port – Road connectivity to ICTT at Vallarpadam Construction of 
subway: The cost of the project is Rs. 30 crore out which Rs.10 crore has 
already been released to the port. In BE 2016 -17 only Rs. 4 crore has be en 
allocated. Considerable progress has been made and the work is likely to be 
completed by 31.08.2016. In case of delay in payment to the contractor, the 
work may come to a standstill. Further being a road project, the public will be 
put to lot of inconve nience. Additional requirement of Rs.16 crore is needed in 
2016-17. 
V. Cochin Port – Rail connectivity to ICTT Vallarpadam : The original cost of the 
project approved by CCEA in March 2007 was Rs. 245.67 crore. Rs. 36.61crore 
was proposed in the BE 2016-17 against which no allocation has been provided. 
The work has been awarded and is scheduled to be completed in September, 
2016. The work is to be funded through GBS as Cochin Port Trust‟s financial 
position doesn‟t permit it to pay the contractor for this work out of its own 
resources. Work may come to standstill if the bills are not cleared. Additional 
requirement of Rs. 36.61crore is needed in 2016-17. 
VI. Setting up of Colachel Satellite Port, along with setting up of Dahanu Port 
submitted to Cabinet for seeking in principle approval:  Feasibility studies have 
been entrusted with regard to the setting up of the port. A some of`  Rs. 96 crore 
was proposed in BE 2016 -17. No allocation has however been provided.  
Additional requirement of Rs.96 crore is needed in 2016-17. 
8

VII. VPT – Financial assistance to VPT for restoration of damages suffered in Hud - 
hud cyclone: Niti Aayog advised that Ministry of Shipping could provide for 
50% of the damages with balance 50% being contributed by the port from its 
internal resources. Rs . 62crore which represents 50% of the damages suffered 
by the Port was proposed in BE 2016 -17. However, no allocation has been 
provided in BE 2016 -17. Additional requirement of Rs. 62crore is needed in 
2016-17. 
26. The Committee takes a serious view of the  fact that the amount allocated 
for the Major Ports are very insignificant compared to the  role and importance of 
the ports in earning revenue for the country and generating employment on large 
scale.  Many of the Major Ports have not got any allocation t his year and some 
ports have got very negligible amount. Many important projects of the Major 
Ports as mentioned by the Ministry of Shipping have been kept aside due to non -
allocation of funds. The Committee notes that the Ports Sector has been allocated 
only Rs. 29 crore wherein various Major Ports require additional fund of Rs. 
388.61 core for meeting the commitments made by them during 2016 -17.  The 
Committee recommends that sufficient fund allocations may be made to the Major 
Ports at the RE stage so th at they can complete the ongoing projects and  the 
projects to be undertaken during 2016-17.

29. The Ministry of Shipping stated that the cargo  throughput of the Major Ports 
increased from 581.34 MT to 606.37 MT in 2015 -16 registering a growth of 4.31 %. 
The ICTT Vallarpadam has improved its pe rformance. In 2015 -16 (April -Feb), the 
terminal handled 3,81,317 TEUs against 3,37,414 TEUs in the same period in 2014 -15, 
displaying a growth of 13.01%. Cochin Port has taken extensive measures to improve 
the container traffic at ICTT by allowing rebates in Vessel Related Charges up to 85% 
of the notified rates for attracting mainline and feeder container ships.   
30. The Committee appreciates the Major Ports like Kolkata, Paradip , 
Kamarajar, V.O. Chidambaranar , Cochin ,Mormugao, Jawaharlal Nehru and 
Kandla  have shown positive growth during 2015-16. The Committee observes that 
even though 8 ports have made positive growth but four major ports have made 
negative figures in cargo handling during this period.   
31. The Committee notes that ICTT Vallarpadam ha s shown some 
improvement in the container handling during 2015 -16 with the efforts of the 
Cochin Port Trust.   The Committee desires that extensive measures are further 
required to make the ICTT an important destination for cargo handling.  The 
Committee also of the view that vigorous marketing of the Vallarpadam Terminal 
at the industrial hubs of the neighboring States need to be done and special tariff 
and smooth container transportation facilities should be provided  for further 
improvement of the cargo traffic at Vallarpadam.

SAGARMALA 
39. The Ministry of Shipping informed that  Sagarmala, a Coastal & Port -led 
Development Programme, is an initiative approved by the Union Cabinet on 25 th 
March, 2015.  It intends to achieve the broad objectives of enhancing the capacity of 
major and non -major ports and modernizing them to make them efficient, thereby 
enabling them to become drivers of port-led economic development, optimizing the use 
of existing and future transport assets and developing new lines/linkages for transport 
(including roads, rail, inland waterways and coastal routes), setting up of logistics hubs, 
and establishment of industries and manufacturing centres to be served by the ports i n 
EXIM and domestic trade.  In addition to strengthening the port and evacuation 
infrastructure, it also aims at simplifying procedures used at ports for cargo movement 
and promotes usage of electronic channels for information exchange leading to quick, 
efficient, hassle -free and seamless cargo movement.  Skill Development of coastal 
communities is also a critical part of Sagarmala initiative.

93. The summary of important audit observations, appearing in the following most 
recent Audit report for the year ended March, 2014 are given below. 
94. Report No.18 of 201 5 Union Government (Civil), Compliance Audit 
Observations : 
(i) Mormugao Port Trust invested Rs.24.28 crore in construction of a berth 
without a detailed feasibility study report which resulted in creating a 
facility which is yet to give any commensurate returns. 
95. Report No.49 of 2015 Union Government, Ministry of Shipping (Performance 
Audit): 
(i) Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) entered into an agreement with 
Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal (NSICT) (July 1997) 
wherein royalty was fixed on per Twenty Foot Equivalent Unit (TEU) 
basis which progressively increased from Rs.47 per TEU (1999-2000) to 
Rs.2670 per TEU (2014 -15).  Due to high royalty rate, the project 
became progressively less remunerative to the operator and threatened 
the viability of the  p roject.  After 18 years of operation, JNPT now 
proposes to migrate from royalty to revenue share mode. 
(ii) While planning for PPP projects in the pre -Model Concession 
Agreement (MCA) period, the ports and the Ministry failed to 
standardize the charges to be sh ared by the p rivate partner, resulting in 
total revenue of Rs.465.95 crore not being shared by the private partner 
at four ports. 
(iii) Cochin Port Trust (CoPT) extended concessions valuing Rs.40.23 crore 
to Dubai Port International (DPI) (concessionaire for Int ernational 
container  Transshipment Terminal (ICTT) due to deviations from 
Request for Qualification (RFQ) terms.  ICTT continued to operate at 35 
per cent capacity since its commissioning in 2011 and the port has not 
reaped any additional return by extension of concession. 
(iv) The implementation of PPP projects suffered from delays between FFQ 
and signing of CAs on account of protracted time taken for finalization 
of tenders, security clearances, litigations etc. Delays in implementation 
of Projects was also o bserved due to non -fulfillment of obligations by 
port authorities relating to appointment of independent engineers, 
obtaining environment clearances, delay in handing over of project sites; 
non provision of committed drought etc.  Delays up to 455 days wer e 
observed on  account on non -fulfillment of conditions precedent by 
concessionaires. 
(v) Though guidelines for monitoring PPP projects issued by Government of 
India envisaged setting up PPP Performance Review Unit (PRU) headed 
by an officer not below the rank of the level of the Central 
Ministry/State  Government/Statutory Entity . Ministry of Shipping 
(MoS) intimated (February 2015) that as an interim arrangement Joint 
Secretary (Ports) in addition to his normal duties, functioned as head of 
PPP-PRU with one PP P expert since October 2012.  A full -fledged PPP 
Cell has now been set  up in the MoS. 
29

(vi) Audit compared the operational efficiency of PPP berths with that of the 
berths at four paras in respect of performance parameters but did not 
notice significant improve ment in the quality of service after 
introduction of PPP model. 
(vii) MCA prescribes the maintenance of Escrow account by the 
concessionaire.  However, as per the order of priority for withdrawal and 
appropriation of funds payment of revenue share was considered  only 
after concessionaire‟s expenses related to operation and management of 
project.  This led to arrears of revenue share to the extent of Rs.41.32 
crore in respect of Berth 13 and 15 and Kandla Port Trust. 
96. Regarding non -inclusion of berth hire charg es in the revenue share, the 
Ministry of shipping replied that the agreement was signed in 1999 before the 
Model Concession Agreement.  So it was not included in the agreement.  
Moreover, this project was approved by the Government in that model before the  
Model Concession Agreement.  Accordingly the Ministry replied to the audit also.  
Now, after the Model Concession Agreement, in all the projects, we are including 
the berth hire charges as a part of the revenue share.   
97. Similarly, regarding the late handing over of the site to the PPP operator the 
Ministry informed the Committee that the matter is in dispute and it is in 
arbitration.  The Port wanted to settle the issue. However,   PPP operator wanted 
additional lengthening of the concession period.  T he port is examining the case 
and  will come out with a proposal to the Government to settle the issue.   
98. Regarding JNPT, in 1999, a concession agreement was entered between 
JNPT and DP World. That was the first concession agreement entered into with a  
private player on a PPP mode in the container terminal.  In that, the revenue share 
model was the royalty.  Per TU, revenue share had to be given by the NSICT to the 
Port Authority.  Subsequently, when the concession agreement came, then, the 
revenue share model came into existence.  During initial years, the rate was fixed 
very low at Rs.40/ - per container.   Over the period, it has increased upto 
Rs.2,800/-. As a result,  the container handling charges have not grew up as 
expected.    Now, the NSICT obje ction is that it is not making profit because it has 
to share Rs.2,800/- per TU with the Port Authority.  In any of these years, NSICT 
has reported a loss.  As Port had no guidance on the concession agreement at the 
time of executing this concession agreem ent,  that remained a problem.  This issue 
has been examined.  The reply has been given to audit on that part because there is 
no real fault exists in that.  However, looking at the pro -active approach, Port 
Board has examined this issue.  The port has appointed M/s E&Y as a consultant to 
examine this.  After examination, that be sent to Ministry of Shipping in a month‟s 
time so that a final decision can be taken about how to restructure that.  As it is a 
concession agreement, if any restructuring has to ha ppen, the port has to follow a 
due legal procedure.

Trust stated that: 
“With regard to International Container Transhipment Terminal (ICTT), 
after the DP World, the concessio naire shifted to Vallarpadam; they had 
built walls around 110 hectares, which was earmarked for them.  But they 
are actually paying lease rent only for 60 hectares.  This issue was written 
to audit and tried to convince audit that they are actually using o nly 60

hectares.  But they have constructed a wall around entire 110 hectares 
because it is got to be a sanitized zone, it is a special economic zone.  On 
the other hand, if the Cochin Port Trust were to build this dividing wall 
between the 60 hectares and the 110 hectares, it would cost us Rs.16 crores

other words,  may be, if it  is given more  funds which shipping sector needs badly,

and capabilities of Shipping sector in our economy in days to come, recommends

 The Committee notes that ICTT Vallarpadam has shown some

Cochin Port Trust.   The Committee desires that extensive measures are further 
required to make the ICTT an important destination for cargo handling.  The 
Committee also of the v iew that vigorous marketing of the Vallarpadam Terminal 
at the industrial hubs of the neighboring States need to be done and special tariff 
and smooth container transportation facilities should be provided  for further 
improvement of the cargo traffic at Vallarpadam.                  (Para:31) 
Port Efficiency Parameters: 
 The Committee notes that compared to 11 th plan period, the capacity of 
the major ports have increased considerably during the 12 th plan period.  As a 
result the major ports have 965 MT capac ities now.  However, the Committee 
is constrained to note that the major ports are utilizing only its 2/3 rd capacity.  
The Committee recommends that alongwith capacity addition measures , the 
major ports should adopt suitable strategies so that its full cap acity could be 
utilized throughout the year.  
(Para:34) 
 The Committee is happy to note that the port efficiency has improved 
now compared to previous years.  The Committee desires that further 
improvement may be observed in the coming years too.                       (Para:35)  
 The Committee notes the various ongoing dredging activities in the Major 
Ports and recommends that completion of the projects may be expedited.                                
(Para:37) 
 The Committee recommends that those Major Ports which have the 
potential for further dredging activities should make their drafts and channels 
able to attract the modern ships/mother ships. The Committee recommends that 
Government should extend necessary budgetary supports to the Major Ports for 
such projects in order to increase the cargo volume in our ports.              (Para:38) 
SAGARMALA 
 The Committee welcomes the Sagarmala project which is intended for an 
integrated development of the In dian Ports and Shipping Sectors. The Committee 
hopes that the project would be able to enhance the capacity of major and non -
major ports and modernizing them to make them efficient, thereby enabling them 
to become drivers of port-led economic development, optimizing the use of existing 
and future transport assets and developing new lines/linkages for  all modes of 
transport, setting up of logistics hubs, and establishment of industries and 
manufacturing centres to be served by the ports in EXIM and domestic trade.                                                                                             
(Para:44) 
 The Committee notes that in order to carry out all the proposed activities 
under Sagarmala, the Ministry requires Rs.1000 crore this year. However , the 
allocation is only Rs.450 crore. The Committee recommends for granting 
additional funds at the RE stage. 
35

(Para:45) 
UPCOMING MAJOR PORTS 
 The Committee desires that the three upcoming Major Ports may be 
completed within the proposed time limit itself as a landmark achievement.                             
(Para:50) 
SHIPPING SECTOR 
 The Committee notes that compared to 2015 -16, the allocation for the 
Shipping and Ship building sector is insufficient as only Rs.48.23 crore has been 
allocated. The Committee  recommends that more allocations may be made at the 
RE stage in view of  major projects planned to be undertaken by the Ministry in 
future.                                (Para:55) 
 The Committee notes the new initiatives  for the Shipping sector as 
communicated by the Ministry and hopes that all the projects may be completed 
as planned by the Ministry.                                                                           (Para:56) 
 The Committee hopes that the ship building subsidy scheme will benefit the 
Indian Shipyards.                                                                                           (Para:57) 
DREDGING CORPORATION OF INDIA LIMITED 
 The Committee recommends that the dues  which is pending for a long time 
from Sethusamudram dredging works need to be paid to DCI  at the earliest so 
that the DCI may be able to increase its dredging volume and machineries. This 
may enable them to harness more dredging orders fr om the major and minor 
ports.                                    (Para:62) 
DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF LIGHTHOUSES & LIGHT SHIPS 
 The Committee understands that DGLL is a revenue making entity under 
the Ministry of Shipping. The Committee desires that the projects tha t have been 
proposed to undertake during 2016-17 shall be completed as per the schedule.                           
(Para:66) 
 The Committee notes that since the lighthouses are located near the 
seashore there may be hindrances for carrying out construction works during the 
monsoon period. The Committee recommends that DGLL may plan the projects 
in such a manner that the works are not get affected by the monsoon.  
                                                                                (Para:67) 
SHIPPING CORPORATION OF INDIA LIMITED 
 The Committee is happy to know that the Shipping Corporation of India 
has now recovered from its loss making phase since 2011 -12 and made a net profit 
of Rs.384.41 crore during 2015 -16. The Committee understands that some of the 
ships owned by the SCI are aged and needed to be phased out. The Co mmittee 
recommends that if the International market situations are viable, they may go for 
purchasing new  fuel efficient vessels in place of the old ones.                                                                                   
(Para:74) 
 
 
36

INLAND WATERWAY AUTHORITY OF INDIA 
 The Committee recommends that cargo movement through the water mode 
need to be entertained in all the viable stretches so that the development of 
national waterways may get a  tremendous boost.   (Para:77) 
 The Committee observes that the development of national waterways as an 
environment friendly and economical alternative mode of transportation of bulk 
cargo is critical for nation building and socio -economic development of various 
regions in the country. Therefore, the Comm ittee recommends that sufficient 
allocations may be made to IWAI for meeting their requirements during 2016-17.                                          
(Para:81) 
JAL MARG VIKAS 
 The Committee recommends that sufficient funds may be allocated for 
timely completion of the project of Jal Marg Vikas.                 (Para:84) 
HOOGHLY DOCK & PORT ENGINEERS LIMITED 
 The Committee recommends that Government should formulate a revival 
plan for saving the HDPEL from incurring regular losses. Since ma ny of the loss 
making PSUs have started making profit, a determined action from the 
Government as well as the employees of the HDPEL may bring profit to it in the 
coming future.                                                                                                 (Para:86) 
CRUISE TOURISM 
 The Committee recommends that IWAI may coordinate with the Ministry 
of Tourism in bringing up all the proposed river tourism projects a reality. In this 
regard, the recommendations made by the  Working Group may be closely 
monitored and necessary steps as required by  the IWAI may be taken at the 
earliest to make the project a success.                                                            (Para:92) 
AUDIT PARA 
 The Committee recommends that all the observations of the audit party 
may be closely examined for fixing the responsibility and remedial actions may be 
taken at the earliest. An action taken note regarding the settlement of all the audit 
paras may also be sent for the information and consideration of the Committee.                                  
(Para:101) 
KOMAGATA MARU MEMORIAL 
 The Committee desires that the Minis try should pursue the matter with 
KMMT to get all the prerequisites for the construction of the Komagata Maru 
Memorial done at the earliest. The Committee may be apprised by sending a 
quarterly report about the progress made in the mater.   (Para:105) 
 The Committee observes that for the new ports, rail connectivity is a big 
issue.  The Indian Port Rail Company can take a pro active role on this issue. For 
a viable project, they can also work with private ports. The Committee 
recommends that the Minis try of Shipping should undertake regular dialogue 
with the Ministry of Railways on this matter and thereby lots of business can be 
generated and given to them by the ports and ultimately port connectivity will 
improve a lot.                                           (Para:106)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf
this Two Hundred Thirty Sixth Report on “Infrastructure Lending in Road Sector”.
2. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
Culture decided to take up the Infrastructure Lending in Road Sector for examination and Report,
as it is felt that roads projects are getting delayed due to various reasons and the Committee tries
to find out the reasons for slow growth of this sector.
3. The Committee heard the views of the Central Engineering Services Group ‘A ’ Officers’
Association, National Highways Builders Federation on the issue on 16th April, 2015.  The
Committee, thereafter, heard the views of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and
National Highways Authority of India on 1st October, 2015.  The Committee also heard the views
of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, National Highways Authority of India,  Ministry
of Finance, Reserve Bank of India, Punjab National Bank and Oriental Bank of Commerce on the
18th February, 2016.
4. The Committee visited Kolkata, Mumbai and Kodaikanal from 31st May to 7th June, 2015
to study the subject i.e. Infrastructure Lending in Road Sector.  The Committee heard the views
of Reserve Bank of India, Union Bank of India, Central Bank of India, State Bank of India, Bank
of Baroda, Bank of India, I.D.B.I., IIFCIL, IFCI, LIC, PERDA, NHAI, Highways Constructors;
Association, Government of Maharashtra at Mumbai on 3rd June, 2015. The Committee also visited
Mumbai and Kochi from 12th 18th October, 2015 and in Kochi the Committee heard the views of
NHAI, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, State Government of Kerala, State Bank of
Travancore, Syndicate Bank on the subject on 17th October, 2015. The Committee also visited
Goa, Hyderabad and Bengaluru from 31st January to 7th February, 2016 and there the Committee
heard the views of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, National Highways Authority of
India, Andhra Bank, State Bank of Hyderabad, Canara Bank, State Bank of Mysore, Vijaya Bank,
States Road Constructors’ Associations.
5. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of Central Engineering Services
Group ‘A’ Officers’ Association, National Highways Builders Federation, Ministry of Road
Transport and Highways and National Highways Authority of India, Ministry of Finance, Reserve
Bank of India, Punjab National Bank and Oriental Bank of Commerce,  Union Bank of India, Central
Bank of India, State Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, Bank of India, I.D.B.I., IIFCIL, IFCI, LIC,
PERDA, Highways Constructors Association, Government of Maharashtra, State Government of
Kerala, State Bank of Travancore, Syndicate Bank, Andhra Bank, State Bank of Hyderabad, Canara
Bank, State Bank of Mysore, Vijaya Bank, States Road Constructors’ Associations and other
stakeholders for placing before the Committee, the material and information desired in connection
with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by the Members.

INTRODUCTION
Availability of an efficient and widespread road network is an essential pre-requisite for a
sustainable economic growth of a country. It is a significant fact that India has the second largest
road network in the world  spread over 5.3 million kilometers, which transports about 60 per cent
of all goods in the country and 85 per cent of overall passenger traffic.  National highways
constitute about 1.9 per cent of road network, but carries about 40 per cent of the total road
traffic. The Ministry of Road, Transport and Highways is primarily responsible for development
and maintenance of National Highways. The main construction programmes implemented by the
Ministry include NHDP (National Highway Development Programme), NH(O) (National Highways
(Original)), Special Accelerated Road Development Programme, Special programme for
Development of Road Connectivity and State Roads in Left Wing Extremism (LWE) Affected Areas
etc.  The Ministry had a target of 10,000 kilometers during the financial year 2015-16. Out of this,
they could achieve a target of 6029 kilometers up to March, 2016. Since the pendency of highways
development projects was increasing and some of important projects were left halfway by the
contractors mainly on account of non availability of regional funds and Banks and other
infrastructure lending institution were feeling reluctant to come forward for financing the highways
sector, the Committee decided to take up the issues related to “lending in road sector for
consideration; to analyze the factors which are hampering the construction of roads and highways.
2. Besides, the Committee took up the issue of infrastructure lending in road sector when it
has noticed that a large number of PPP projects were languishing or delayed due to various reasons
and there were hardly any taker for PPP Projects.
3. The Committee interacted with public sector banks, financial institutions, RBI, Governmental
agencies, NHAI, Ministry of Road, Transport and Highways, Ministry of Finance, Highways
Builders’ Association and Federations on the infrastructure lending in road sector. While examining
the infrastructure lending in road sector, the Committee  noticed various problems and bottlenecks
in infrastructure lending such as need for policy measures to give fillip to infrastructure
development; regulatory measures to facilitate the flow of bank credit to infrastructure sector;
financing requirements of infrastructure sector; asset management issues for the banks; delays in
commercial operations vis-à-vis infrastructure lending; problem of sector-wise exposure ceiling vis-à-vis
lending by Banks to infrastructure sector; problem and issues relating to funding of PPP projects;
environmental clearance and other statutory clearances; slow down of economy and infrastructure
lending; role of NHAI, State and Central agencies; corporate bonds and infrastructure lending and
exposure of Financial Institutions/Banks to Infrastructure Sector and NPAs.

EXISTING MODELS FOR ROAD CONSTRUCTION
16. The Committee was informed by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways that there
are three models viz. EPC model, PPP Mode and Hybrid Annuity model for construction of roads.
17. (i) EPC Model:  The EPC (engineering, procurement and construction) model entails that the
contractor builds the project by designing, installing and procuring necessary labour and land to
construct the infrastructure, either directly or by subcontracting. Unlike PPP, the financing is done
by the Government and not by banks or private equity funds through issuing of sovereign bonds
or taking financial guarantees for the project. Government also takes responsibility for land
procurement, clearances, etc. Recently, the Government has announced that it will focus on
developing upcoming road project on EPC mode for the coming two years rather than PPP (public
private partnership) mode. The shift to EPC mode is due to the fact that PPP modes are
economically not viable at this moment. However, the cons of this model is that it may entail huge
budgetary support which increases the fiscal deficit.
(ii) PPP Model: Under PPP (public private partnership) model Government agencies tie up
with private agencies for development of infrastructure. In case of highway projects in India,
National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) acts as the project authority while projects are
executed by various private agencies known as concessionaire. These concessionaires, apart from
putting their own equity, depend heavily on bank finance. Revenue under this model to the

7
concessionaire can be derived either by direct collection of toll by the concessionaire or by
payment of annuities to the concessionaire by the Government.   In the event of project delays,
or shortfall in collection of toll, the risk of default to the lenders arises. The pros of this model
is that direct fiscal burden on Government is avoided as well as the project may get more
professional expertise of private sector. On the negative side, in cases of delayed implementation,
private players aren’t able to service their loans, adding to NPAs in banks, eventually
disincentivising banks from lending for such projects.
(iii) Hybrid Annuity Model: The hybrid annuity model was conceived in the previous
financial year 2015-16 to bring back private participation in highway projects, which had dried up
in the last few years. The model is a mix of EPC and BOT *formats, with the Government and
the private enterprise sharing the total project cost in the ratio of 40:60, respectively. Under this
new model, Government provides 40% of the project cost during the construction period and the
release of funds is linked to the progress of construction.
18. The private player needs to raise the rest 60% in the form of equity and loan. Since the
overall requirement is less, the private bidder needs to put less equity. Similarly, as the loan
requirement is less in comparison to the other modes such as PPP, banks will also be comfortable
to lend. Government pays back the rest in installments during the entire contract period and it is
linked to the performance of the private player and the asset.
19. The recovery of entire investment is assured as Government takes all the risks including
collecting user fee and thereby the rise or fall in the total collections does not impact the private
participant’s return from the project. It brings greater comfort to the private players and banks to
take up such projects.

REASONS RESPONSIBLE FOR LANGUISHING PROJECTS:
25. Ministry has cited following reasons responsible for languishing projects:
(i) Lack of equity with the Concessionaire:  In projects (e.g. Motihari-Raxaul section,
Rohtak – Jind section, Gurgaon – Kotputli – Jaipur section, Haridwar – Dehradun
section), the lack of equity with the concessionaires has delayed the projects much
beyond the scheduled completion date. In some projects, this has also resulted in the
bankers not disbursing even the loan sanctioned at Financial Close.
(ii)   Diversion of Funds: In few cases the physical progress of work is not
commensurate with the financial progress. These are likely cases where the funds
may not have been utilized towards the projects and concessionaires are finding it
difficult to bring back the funds so diverted.
(iii)  Delays due to reasons not attributable to the Concessionaire: The Authority has
also defaulted in fulfillment of its conditions precedent in a number of cases due to
Land Acquisition, Environment/Forest clearance/Utility Shifting/RoB issues. In cases
like Rimoli – Roxy – Rajamunda, due to delay in forest clearance the project has
turned non viable and requires to be terminated and rebid.
(iv)    Refusal of banks to accept first charge of NHAI:  For any languishing highway
project in BOT (Toll/Annuity) mode that has achieved at least 50% physical
completion, NHAI will provide financial assistance to complete the project subject
to first charge on the Toll/Annuity receivables of these projects. However, the banks
have refused to accept the first charge of NHAI and therefore no progress in
implementation of this policy to complete languishing projects is being achieved.
(v)   High Cost of Interest during Construction (IDC): The cost of construction in
case of delay whether due to concessionaire or the Authority, results in increase in
the cost of debt which turns the project unviable. In case of termination due to
delay by concessionaire during the construction period, there is also no termination
payment.
(vi)  Difficulty in obtaining additional debt in stalled projects: In projects where the
concessionaire is already faced with delays, there is no possibility of obtaining
additional debt to complete the project as the account in many cases may have
already turned NPA.

(vii) Overleveraged Balance sheet of the developers anticipating high level of
growth: The economic downturn seen in the last few years has caused revenue
realization at a much lower rate than was anticipated.   Many developers have taken
future obligation which created difficulties in debt servicing.
(viii) Stress on the existing road infrastructure loan portfolios of FIs:  Reduced
revenue realization due to economic slowdown affecting debt servicing  by the
Concessionaire as the contracted debt servicing   obligations   could not be met with
the existing revenue. As the sector got affected, the lenders debt portfolio for roads
came to have a disproportionally high level of debts.  NPAs saddled banks with
additional capital adequacy requirements, provisioning demands and income
recognition restrictions.
(ix) Long period of revenue collection : The current practice of financing large
infrastructure projects based on revenue streams spread over 20 to 30 years, but
with project debt having tenure of 10 to 15 years, is also unsustainable.
(x) Debt sanctioned by Banks higher than total project cost estimated by NHAI:
Because the project debt is based on the developer’s cost estimates that is, on
average, higher by 35 per cent than the NHAI project cost. In such cases, the
lenders are exposed to a higher risk particularly in the event of termination of the
Concession Agreement wherein NHAI guarantees compensation based on its own
appraised project cost and not the developer’s estimate.
(xi) Corporate Debt Restructuring has been affected in many SPV debt:
Concessionaire unable to service debt have to propose to the lenders  to restructure
the debt:  While the first restructuring  exercise is permitted by lenders without any
adverse asset classifications any such second exercise automatically affect the asset
classifications in the books of lenders. Any second restructuring necessarily requires
that the debt be classified as non performing.
(xii) Sector exposure norms of FIs getting exhausted:  With the debt obligations
mounting on account of debt repayment deferment, sector exposure increased,
reaching exposure norms for this sector.
(xiii) Higher cost of financing:  The lenders who provide major part of financing in the
form of debt are concerned with the downside risks which influences the project
progress and debt serving capability  and consequently to mitigate the risk of
financing have enhanced the cost of lending to the sector.
(xiv) Bond Market for infrastructure financing:  The Bond market can provide a
viable option for long term financing. Under the Infrastructure Debt Fund,  Banks
have to accept the first charge of Infrastructure Debt Funds on termination
payment. As projects have been financed at a much higher cost than the NHAI total
project cost, the debt due may not cover the complete senior debt leading to
resistance of banks to first charge of Infrastructure Debt Funds.

BANKS’ LIMIT FOR LONG TERM LOAN
26. The Deputy Governor, RBI submitted before the Committee that the assets in which bank
invest and the advances or loans which they give, there is a limit to their length. So, typically,
banks give it for seven years, whereas these are projects which require financing for 20 or 25
years. Banks have inherent limitations for that kind of long-term financing. Elsewhere, it is not
bank-funded. It is all market-funding or Government-funding only, and the banks will have only
fringe way of doing it. But in our country, as the country demanded that kind of support from
the banking system, the banking system rose to the occasion. In 2007-08, for the entire
infrastructure projects, the funding by the banks was to the tune of `2,00,000 crores, but today
it is `10,00,000 crores plus. So, in these years, the banks have risen five times to support it. That
is why it cannot be done beyond the limit. This itself is forming part of 16 per cent of their total
assets. Banks have to give 40 per cent to the priority sector; 21 per cent they have to put in SLR
bonds and Government securities and four per cent as CRR. Putting all these together, it comes
to 81 per cent. The remaining funds are available for the rest of the business through which they
are supposed to make extra funds and other things.
27. Deputy Governor RBI in his submission before the Committee added that they have allowed
the banks to take long-term bonds on which exemption is given from SLR, CRR, etc. This kind
of enablement will have to be for the right size. That is why the size has been fixed at `500
crores. So, `500 crores is the requirement, based on which all these enablements, all these facilities
or exemptions from SLR, CRR, etc., are feasible. If banks start giving for `200 crores or any less
amount, then, they will not get the required generation of funds. They have to generate revenue.
The remaining 19 per cent only is available for them to take big money. Then the interest rate for
that portion will have to be much, much higher. So, there is a need of balancing.
28. When queried if the threshold limit is brought down for 500 crores to 200 or 300 crores,
how it would affect, RBI said that if the threshold limit is brought down then the bank will have
to extend the recovery of those project loans for twenty years.  As a result, every year the interest
rate flow and the cash flow which is coming back to the banks will be less and they will not be
able to do the rest of the funding.
29. In view of this, the Committee urges RBI to look into the matter and if possible
threshold limit should be brought down so that some more projects could also be completed
which needs lesser amount.
NON PERFORMING ASSETS (NPA)
30. The Chairman, NHAI submitted that loan accounts having an interest or scheduled payment
overdue, where the payment overdue is more than 90 days, are today classified as NPAs. So, once
a loan is declared as NPA, it is not possible for him to secure loans from other banks and financial
institutions. Economic slowdown has resulted in significant decline in traffic levels. The toll rates
have come down because toll rates are linked to the wholesale price index. As a result  toll rates,
sometimes, go negative. So, RBI is requested to relax the NPA norms to 180 days; perhaps, at
one time, they had 180 days as the norm.  This will provide developers more time to work out
an arrangement for regularization of their account and also reduce the cost of funds for the
banks.

COMMENTS OF RBI ON NPA
31. Regarding NPA, RBI said that  ’90 days’ is a part of international guidelines for identifying
an NPA.  This is accounting concept in the sense that if a party is not paying back either interest
or installment from the due date within next ninety days, then, the bank should not recognize
income because nothing is coming and when it is not coming, it cannot be recognized that interest
has come or the installment has come.  That becomes NPA.  Because of this problem, it is again
and again reiterated that even though it is an NPA, the bank should fund it so long as it is a viable
project.  Since India has signed the Basel Convention and it is mandatory to adhere to the guideline,
90 days’ period cannot be relaxed.
